scope: Four original AS Chemistry 3.1.3 drawing/reasoning problems worth 26 marks (actual diagrams manually checked)
notes: Hand-drawn content has no automated grading. All mark points are a transparent manual rubric, not an official AQA mark scheme. Drawings are representations of structures, no experimental procedures.

questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.question: Sketch and explain a sodium chloride ionic lattice
questions.subtopic: Ionic lattice, metal lattice, coordinate bonds, giant covalent networks
questions.prompt: Draw a labelled two-dimensional section of the giant ionic structure of solid NaCl showing at least four Na⁺ ions and four Cl⁻ ions alternating in adjacent positions. Label charges and explain why solid NaCl cannot conduct electricity but molten NaCl can. Your drawing must be marked from the actual sketch. [6 marks]
markPoints: Sketch represents an extended, repeating arrangement, not isolated NaCl molecules.
Depicts at least four Na⁺ and four Cl⁻ ions with the stated charges.
Shows neighbouring ions of opposite charge in the lattice section.
Explains strong electrostatic attraction in all directions between oppositely charged ions.
Explains solid ions cannot move, so no charge carriers flow despite charged ions.
Explains ions are mobile in molten NaCl, permitting electrical conduction.
questions.modelAnswer: A 2D section can show alternating Na⁺ and Cl⁻ lattice positions, at least four of each, with neighbouring opposite charges. The extended structure is held together by strong electrostatic forces in all directions. In a solid the ions are fixed, so charge cannot travel through the lattice; in the molten state the ions can move and carry charge. Manually inspect all drawn ions and labels.

questions.question: Sketch the metallic bonding model for magnesium
questions.subtopic: Ionic lattice, metal lattice, coordinate bonds, giant covalent networks
questions.prompt: Draw a labelled model of solid magnesium showing a regular arrangement of positive metal ions and the delocalised electrons. Explain why metallic bonding enables good electrical conductivity and why the metal can be shaped without the entire lattice breaking. Use the actual diagram for manual mark-point review. [7 marks]
markPoints: Sketch shows a regular array/lattice of positive metal ions, not neutral molecules.
Labels the ions as positive (Mg²⁺ is acceptable in the simple metallic bonding model).
Draws or labels a sea of delocalised electrons distributed between the ions.
Explains electrostatic attraction between the mobile electrons and the positive metal-ion lattice constitutes metallic bonding.
Explains mobile delocalised electrons transport charge in solid magnesium.
States layers of metal ions can slide/rearrange under mechanical stress.
Explains electron–ion attraction is non-directional so metallic bonding persists as layers move.
questions.modelAnswer: Draw repeating rows of positive magnesium ions (e.g. labelled Mg²⁺), with delocalised electrons between and around them. Metallic bonding is electrostatic attraction between the positive lattice and the delocalised electrons. Mobile electrons carry current without ion motion in solid magnesium. When the metal is bent or hammered, ionic layers can slide while the electron sea continues to hold the lattice together. The diagram must be judged by manual inspection.

questions.question: Draw and explain a dative bond from ammonia
questions.subtopic: Ionic lattice, metal lattice, coordinate bonds, giant covalent networks
questions.prompt: Draw NH₃ with its nitrogen lone pair and show how NH₃ bonds to H⁺ to form NH₄⁺. Use a directional dative bond arrow and identify the origin of the electron pair. State the final molecular shape and an approximate H–N–H bond angle in ammonium. The answer requires actual drawn bonds. [6 marks]
markPoints: Shows NH₃ nitrogen bonded to three H atoms with a lone pair on N.
Shows H⁺ as the accepting species rather than a neutral H atom supplying an electron.
Draws a dative arrow from nitrogen/lone pair towards H⁺ (not the reverse).
Explains that both shared electrons of the new co-ordinate bond are donated by N.
Shows the product NH₄⁺ with four N–H bonds and overall + charge.
Names tetrahedral shape and approximate 109.5° bond angle around N in NH₄⁺.
questions.modelAnswer: Sketch NH₃ with three N–H covalent bonds and one lone pair on N. Draw N: → H⁺, the arrow pointing from nitrogen to the H⁺ acceptor. Both bonding electrons originally come from nitrogen's lone pair. Draw [NH₄]⁺ with four equivalent N–H bonds. There are four bonding pairs and no lone pairs on N in the ammonium ion, giving tetrahedral geometry with angles of about 109.5°. Diagram marking is manual.

questions.question: Compare diamond and graphite bonding diagrams
questions.subtopic: Ionic lattice, metal lattice, coordinate bonds, giant covalent networks
questions.prompt: Sketch one carbon atom's covalent neighbours in diamond and one carbon atom's covalent neighbours in a graphite layer, using labels or a simple extended framework. Explain the differences in their electrical conductivity and why graphite layers can slide. Your diagram labels must be checked manually. [7 marks]
markPoints: Diamond sketch shows each central carbon bonded to FOUR carbon neighbours in a 3D tetrahedral giant covalent network.
Graphite sketch shows each carbon bonded to THREE neighbours in a planar hexagonal layer.
Identifies diamond as a giant covalent/macromolecular lattice.
Explains diamond has no mobile delocalised electrons or ions, so it is normally non-conducting.
Identifies graphite as a layered giant covalent lattice with one electron per carbon delocalised within the layer.
Explains graphite conducts along layers owing to mobile delocalised electrons.
Explains only weak forces between graphite layers, allowing layers to slide relative to one another.
questions.modelAnswer: Draw diamond carbon with four covalent bonds in a three-dimensional tetrahedral network. Draw graphite as a planar hexagonal sheet with each C bonded to three neighbours; one remaining valence electron per carbon contributes to delocalised charge. Diamond has no mobile charge carriers, so it is normally an insulator. Graphite's delocalised electrons make it conductive along the sheets, while weak interlayer forces allow the layers to slide. All drawing criteria require manual inspection.
